# Architecture

High-level map of the current Daedalus implementation. For build commands and coding conventions see [Copilot instructions](../copilot-instructions.md); planned work and audit status belong in [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md). Source and runtime paths below are relative to the repository root.

## Projects

| Project | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `dlEngine` | `source/dlEngine` | Shared engine library, assembled from static module libraries (exports via `DAEDALUS_API`) |
| `dlSandbox` | `source/dlSandbox` | Client executable; implements `CreateApplication()` (`SandboxApp.cpp`) and loads a configured runtime scene |
| `dlUnitTests` | `source/dlUnitTests` | gtest suite, one executable (`-DENABLE_TESTS=ON`) |
| shaders | `source/shader` | GLSL shaders loaded at runtime |

The client links the engine; `Core/EntryPoint.h` supplies the executable entry point and calls the client's `CreateApplication()`.

The root CMake project requires C++20 and supports Windows and Linux. Each engine module is a static library linked privately into `dlEngine`; whole-archive linking on MSVC and Linux retains public APIs without internal callers. This is one shared engine library, not independently loaded module plugins. Debug and ReleaseDevTools enable `DL_DEV_TOOLS`; Release is the production configuration. Binaries are emitted under `runtime/bin/<platform>-x64`, and build steps copy shaders to `runtime/shader`. Source files are registered explicitly in each target's `CMakeLists.txt`.

## Engine modules (`source/dlEngine`)

| Module | Responsibility | Key files |
|---|---|---|
| `Core` | Application, Engine ownership, asset registry/pipeline, layers, window and input interfaces | `Application`, `Engine`, `AssetRegistry`, `AssetPipeline`, `Layer`, `LayerStack`, `Window`, `Input`, `EntryPoint.h` |
| `Config` | INI-backed settings (SimpleIni), typed runtime CVar bindings | `GraphicsConfig`, `KeybindConfig`, `PathConfig`, `CVarRegistry`, `ConfigCVars` |
| `Debug` | Logging with category/level filtering, CPU/GPU profiler, ImGui debug UI and build-information reporting | `Log`, `Profiler`, `ProfileScope`, `ProfilerStats`, `ImGuiLayer`, `DebugOverlay`, `ConsoleOverlay`, `BuildInfo` |
| `Events` | Thread-safe enqueue, owner-thread dispatch, event types | `Event`, `EventDispatcher`, `EventsEngine`, `EventTable` |
| `Threads` | Engine-owned dependency scheduler, worker pool, main-thread jobs and thread-lifetime helpers | `JobSystem`, `JobHandle`, `ThreadRunner`, `ThreadPool`, `ThreadJoiner`, `DaedalusThreads` |
| `Platform` | OS and windowing backends behind abstractions | `Platform.h`, `GLFW/`, `Windows/`, `Linux/`, `OpenGL/` |
| `Renderer` | Deferred renderer, passes, developer debug drawing, GPU resources, caches and statistics | `API/`, `Debug/DebugDrawBatch`, `Objects/`, `Passes/`, `Primitives/`, `Resources/` |
| `ECS` | Scene management, EnTT entities, native scripts, systems and scene persistence | `SceneManager`, `Scene`, `Entity`, `Components.h`, `NativeScriptComponent`, `NativeScripts/`, `Systems/`, `Serialization/` |
| `Physics` | Engine-owned world factory and independent Bullet worlds | `Physics`, `PhysicsWorld` |
| `Utils` | Small shared utilities and named virtual filesystem mounts | `Timer`, `DeltaTime`, `FixedStepClock`, `FPSLocker`, `RingVector`, `VirtualFileSystem`, `KeyCodes`, `WorkingDirectory` |

The developer console supports `help`, `clear`, `quit` and `version`, plus the CVar and input commands described below. `help` lists every supported command alphabetically with syntax and a short description; extra arguments produce `Usage: help`. `Debug/ConsoleCommands` shares one graphics-independent catalog between help output and command-name Tab completion/inline hints. Detailed input rules remain available through `input_help`. `version` prints application version, build version, build configuration, target platform/architecture, compiler/version and developer-tools status through `Debug/GetBuildInfo()`. Application and build versions both use the existing `major.minor.patch` value from `version.txt`, without a separate build counter. The helper needs no window or graphics context and formats its report only when requested. `version.txt` is parsed once by `CMakeScripts/Version.cmake` for both packaging and embedded application metadata; changing it triggers CMake regeneration. Build metadata describes the compiled binary, not the host running it, and excludes timestamps and Git revisions.

Runtime configuration (`Config/CVarRegistry`): an instance-owned, owner-thread registry binds stable-type `bool`, `int`, `float` and string getters to optional validated setters. The developer console owns its registry and calls `RegisterConfigCVars` after Config initialization; callbacks must not outlive Config. `cvars [prefix]` lists sorted names, values, descriptions and runtime/read-only status; `get <name>` reads the current value; `set <name> <value>` validates before mutation. Numeric parsing rejects overflow, trailing text and nonfinite floats; booleans accept `true`, `false`, `1` and `0`. String values keep internal spaces without quote processing. Completion resolves command names or CVar names in the first argument. While the input is focused with an end-of-text cursor and no selection, muted inline text shows the untyped suffix of the first alphabetically matching name; Tab accepts that suffix. Blank input, values, unmatched/exact names and suggestions exceeding the input buffer have no hint. Mid-line Tab completion retains following value text; ambiguous mid-line matches are listed rather than inserted. `Debug/ConsoleCompletion` supplies graphics-independent matching and hint rules. The console caches hints until text/cursor/selection changes and uses ImGui's internal input scroll offset only in rendering to align clipped ghost text with horizontally scrolled input.

`graphics.fps_lock` is writable (`0` disables limiting; negative values are rejected) and is consumed by the existing per-frame FPS locker. `keybind.<name>` bindings are registered from the existing keyboard map at console initialization, validate GLFW keyboard codes and take effect through live keybind queries. Other exposed `graphics.*` settings and `paths.assets`, `paths.shaders`, `paths.config`, `paths.logs`, `paths.scene` are read-only: changing startup-baked GPU/window/mount state is not implied by changing an INI value. Runtime CVar edits use the existing Config save on engine teardown; CVar registration does not support automatic INI reload, new-key creation, gamepad rebinding or renderer-setting rebuild. Input commands described below provide action creation and gamepad rebinding separately. Registry registration rejects duplicate/invalid names; names use letters, digits, underscore and dot.

### Input actions and rebinding

Engine-owned `KeybindConfig` supplies persistent bindings to the static `Input` facade on the application thread. Existing `[Keyboard] name=code` entries also define named actions; optional `[Gamepad] name=button` entries combine a gamepad button with the same action. `InputActionBinding` uses `-1` for an unbound keyboard key or gamepad button. `SetActionBind`, `SetAxisBind`, `FindActionBind`, `FindAxisBind` and const binding-map accessors provide code-level registration, inspection and rebinding. Legacy `SetKeyboardBind` preserves the gamepad binding. Names are case-sensitive, 1–64 ASCII letters/digits/underscore/dot; invalid names/codes/axis references are rejected without mutation. INI parsing rejects malformed, overflowed, nonfinite or trailing input and warns while retaining existing entries. Loads merge valid entries, including legacy keyboard-only files. Config saves all three sections on normal engine teardown. Returned map pointers/references are non-owning; do not retain them across edits/load or Config destruction. No automatic file reload is implemented.

`[Axes] name=negative-action positive-action gamepad-axis scale deadzone` stores `InputAxisBinding`; `-` omits a digital direction and axis `-1` omits analog input. Axis codes are 0 LeftX, 1 LeftY, 2 RightX, 3 RightY, 4 LeftTrigger, 5 RightTrigger. Direction names must refer to existing actions. Finite scale in `[-1,1]` affects analog only; deadzone is in `[0,1)`. `GetAxis` subtracts negative action-down from positive action-down, adds scaled analog input and clamps to `[-1,1]`. Sticks remain signed, triggers normalize raw `[-1,1]` to `[0,1]`, and magnitudes inside the deadzone are zero with the remainder rescaled to full range. Nonfinite backend axis samples are neutral. Axis edits are read directly by `GetAxis`.

`Input::Update` samples the GLFW keyboard and first gamepad (`GLFW_JOYSTICK_1`) once per frame before queued-event dispatch. Fixed arrays avoid invalid backend indices and per-frame state allocation; disconnection clears buttons/sticks and resets raw triggers to `-1`. Named state storage grows only when actions are added, using Config revision tracking. `IsActionDown` is continuous; `IsActionPressed`, `IsActionHold`, and `IsActionReleased` use aggregate keyboard-or-gamepad transitions, are not consumed by queries, and remain frame-based even across multiple fixed ticks. Holding either device prevents a release when the other releases. Changed/new action bindings establish an edge baseline at the next input update without manufacturing a press/release. Keyboard/gamepad enable gates apply immediately to named queries and axes; raw gamepad queries also honor the gamepad gate, which currently defaults enabled. GLFW connection notifications do not change this explicit gate; frame polling neutralizes disconnected devices. Gate changes recompute the current action value without advancing its previous-frame state. The legacy raw button method `IsGpadKeyPressed` remains a continuous down query, and enabled raw triggers retain their original `[-1,1]` convention. Stick deadzone configuration rejects nonfinite/out-of-range values; named axes use their own deadzones.

Developer-console `actions [prefix]` and `axes [prefix]` list sorted live mappings. `bind_action <name> <keyboard-code|-1> <gamepad-button|-1>` creates/replaces an action. `bind_axis <name> <negative-action|-> <positive-action|-> <gamepad-axis|-1> <scale> <deadzone>` creates/replaces an axis. `input_help` describes syntax, codes and persistence. `Debug/InputCommands` handles these without a graphics context; malformed commands leave Config unchanged. Command/first-binding-name Tab completion and inline hints use live maps and invalidate cached hints on binding revision changes. Existing `keybind.*` CVars still snapshot names at console initialization and require concrete keyboard codes; new commands support action creation, gamepad rebinding and explicit unbinding independently of that snapshot. There is no interactive capture UI, multiple-gamepad selection, mouse mapping, chords, action contexts or automatic gameplay-axis registration.

`CameraController` and the example `PlayerControllerScript` consume signed left-stick X/right and negative Y/forward independently of button actions. Without named movement axes, forward/backward/left/right digital movement reads only the configured keyboard keys through `IsKeyHold`, preserving keyboard Hold timing independently of any already-held gamepad button. Planar action button bindings are not consumed by these default script paths, so sharing B between MoveForward and ChangePOV or A between MoveLeft and Console does not cause movement. Bindings themselves are unchanged; action queries elsewhere still expose those buttons, and camera MoveUp/MoveDown retain aggregate `IsActionHold` behavior. Codes 0/1 remain A/B in action bindings, not LeftX/LeftY. Camera stick translation retains magnitude and its existing 10-units/second multiplier; right-stick look and mouse controls are unchanged. Player facing combines the same weighted camera-relative movement, projects it onto the horizontal plane and retains the existing yaw turn-rate limit; neutral sticks do not change facing. Explicit axes named `MoveHorizontal` (positive right) and `MoveVertical` (positive forward) opt in per component and replace both that component's keyboard movement and raw left-stick path, avoiding double-counting. They retain full `GetAxis` semantics, including aggregate action-down/button input, deadzone rescaling, analog scale and clamping; explicitly mapping a shared button into such an axis can still activate it. Typical `[Axes]` entries are `MoveHorizontal=MoveLeft MoveRight 0 1 0.15` and `MoveVertical=MoveBackward MoveForward 1 -1 0.15`, provided those actions exist and their digital button mappings are intentional. Scripts do not create axes, reinterpret action button codes or overwrite user bindings. Example Flashlight/ChangePOV toggles use aggregate action release edges.

Debug drawing (`Renderer/Debug/DebugDrawBatch`): the static Renderer facade exposes `DebugLine`, axis-aligned `DebugBox` and three-great-circle `DebugSphere`. Submissions are graphics-thread-only, world-space, opaque RGB in `[0, 1]`, and return whether the complete primitive was accepted. Depth-tested and overlay lines share a 4,096-line frame budget; spheres use 3–128 segments per circle (default 32). Invalid/nonfinite geometry and over-budget shapes are rejected atomically. CPU vectors are reserved once and GPU vertex storage is reused, with no per-submission/frame growth. `GetRejectedDebugPrimitives` reports the last flushed frame's rejected submissions.

In developer builds, `Application::Run` starts the debug batch before events/fixed update/update and flushes it after scene, skybox and layer rendering, before ImGui. Lines use the last completed scene pipeline's camera/scene UBO and the copied geometry depth; depth-tested lines draw first, overlay lines last, without depth writes. A frame with no completed camera discards its submissions rather than using stale matrices. Submissions after the final flush (including ImGui) are cleared at the next frame start. The OpenGL backend restores changed program/VAO/array-buffer/framebuffer bindings, depth state, color masks, line width and affected capabilities. `shaders:/DebugDraw.glsl` supplies the shader through the normal shader library/hot-reload path; if unavailable, the frame is discarded with a warning rather than an asserting lookup. No duration-based primitives, text, arbitrary triangles, multiple-view routing or automatic Bullet debug-draw adapter are implemented. Release facade calls return false/no-op without accessing a renderer, and allocate no debug batch/GPU storage; the graphics-independent batch remains available for tests and tools.

Profiler (`Debug/Profiler`): `DL_PROFILE_SCOPE(name)` records RAII CPU scopes (static names, thread id, depth) into a bounded per-frame buffer; `Application::Run` brackets each frame with `Profiler::BeginFrame`/`EndFrame` and instruments events, scene commit, fixed update, update, render, ImGui, swap and FPS lock. `Profiler::StartCapture`/`StopCapture` exports Chrome trace JSON; only an active capture allocates per frame. Scene update/fixed update/render, native scripts, `RenderSystem` (model submission, skybox), `PhysicsSystem` (step, transform sync), `PhysicsWorld::StepSimulation` and every `RenderPass` (named via `RenderPass::GetName()`) are also instrumented. Scope names use the `Class::Method` form (e.g. `Application::Update`, `RenderSystem::RenderSkybox`).

GPU timing: in dev builds the renderer owns a `GPUTimer` (abstraction in `Renderer/Primitives`, OpenGL implementation `Platform/OpenGL/OpenGLGPUTimer`). `Application::Run` brackets render + ImGui with `Renderer::BeginGpuProfileFrame`/`EndGpuProfileFrame`; `DL_PROFILE_GPU_SCOPE(name)` (RAII `GpuProfileScope` in `Renderer.h`, no-op without `DL_DEV_TOOLS`) times `Application::Render`, each pass in `Renderer::FlushPipeline`, `Renderer::CopyDepth`, `Renderer::ComputeDebugInfo`, `RenderSystem::RenderSkybox` and `Application::ImGui`. The timer keeps a ring of 4 frames of `GL_TIMESTAMP` queries and reads results only when available, so it never stalls the CPU; results arrive a few frames late via `Profiler::SubmitGpuSamples`. Each frame samples `GL_TIMESTAMP` with `glGetInteger64v` together with the profiler clock, and that offset converts GPU timestamps onto the profiler clock so GPU scopes line up with CPU scopes in traces. Frames whose results are still unavailable when their slot is reused are discarded and counted via `Profiler::ReportDroppedGpuFrame`.

`ProfilerStats` aggregates consecutive frames into per-scope call count, last/avg/p95/p99/max and a 240-frame history (allocates only for newly seen scope names). The profiler owns the CPU and GPU stats and updates them in `EndFrame`/`SubmitGpuSamples`, so history is continuous whether or not the UI is open; `Profiler::CopyStats` snapshots them. The Profiler tab in `DebugOverlay` shows a frame-time graph, a sortable per-frame sample table (unsorted keeps call hierarchy), sortable CPU/GPU scope tables with per-scope history, the dropped GPU frame count and capture controls. Text refreshes every 0.5 s for readability; the view can be paused with a checkbox or by holding Ctrl.

`DebugOverlay` is the debug-window coordinator: it owns window sizing, top-level tab headers, visibility/input handling and one-time style scaling. It creates five uniquely owned concrete tab classes during initialization under `Debug/Tabs`: `GeneralDebugTab` owns monitoring histories and hardware metadata; `RenderingDebugTab` owns framebuffer previews; `ResourcesDebugTab` owns resource inspection; `ProfilerDebugTab` owns profiling snapshots, sorting and pause/capture UI; `LoggingDebugTab` owns log output and filters. Only the selected tab renders, nested tabs remain inside their parent tab, and profiling collection remains owned by `Profiler` independently of the UI. The coordinator retains the Logging tab's fixed-size window policy.

In developer builds, `ConsoleOverlay` and `DebugOverlay` toggle on keyboard release or `GpadReleasedEvent` matching the live `Console` and `Debug` action bindings respectively. Missing/unbound gamepad bindings are ignored; gamepad press/repeat events do not toggle either window. Keyboard and gamepad handlers share the existing visibility/cursor update path; closing the console also restores its typing-related keyboard-input gate. No default gamepad bindings are created.

The initial profiler implementation is complete as a CPU/GPU timing profiler. It does not intercept or attribute memory allocations. General-tab RAM readings and Resources-tab memory estimates are separate usage summaries, not allocation profiling. Optional future profiler work, including memory profiling, is tracked in `ROADMAP.md` and is not part of the implemented architecture.

## Application lifecycle

`Application` owns one `Engine`. Engine owns concrete configuration, input, job-scheduler, asset-pipeline, renderer, resource-manager, physics-factory, event-queue and scene-manager instances. Static facades such as `Renderer::` and `Input::` refer to these instances without owning them; calls outside their lifetime fail fast. Only one active application/service set is supported. Logging remains a bootstrap service available before Engine construction and after Engine shutdown.

Construction order:
1. Install platform failure handling and create Engine's configuration instances; load configs.
2. Create input and the window/context from `GraphicsConfig` via `Platform`.
3. Construct the job scheduler, mount configured folders and initialize the asset registry. Inject the scheduler into the resource manager before creating the renderer (renderer initialization can load resources), then load shaders and connect shader-change notifications.
4. Start the event queue and register a window callback that clones payloads into it.
5. Attach the ImGui overlay; dev builds also attach debug and console windows. Client layers may request a loaded scene for activation on the next frame boundary.

Main loop (`Application::Run`):
1. Poll window events, update input, and dispatch the queued event snapshot on the application thread.
2. Pump bounded ready main-thread jobs, schedule the asset poll when due, then commit a pending scene switch; purge resources no longer externally referenced.
3. Run fixed scene/physics and layer updates at approximately 60 Hz (`FixedStepClock`). Catch-up is limited to eight ticks per frame; excess elapsed time after a stall is deliberately dropped.
4. Run variable layer updates and scene scripts, then scene/layer rendering.
5. Begin one ImGui frame, invoke layer UI hooks, and render ImGui once.
6. Swap buffers and apply frame limiting via `FPSLocker`.

Shutdown rejects new job submissions and drains accepted jobs, including main-thread continuations, before rejecting queued events and destroying managed scenes while client layers still exist. Layers detach next; ImGui saves its config before destroying its context. Engine then destroys systems in reverse ownership order, preserving the graphics context until renderer and cache destruction finish. Its configuration session saves ordinary settings last. `Application::GetInstance()` is cleared after Engine destruction. Job producers must finish before Engine destruction; job captures must not outlive the resources they access.

## Layers

A `Layer` receives fixed-update, update, render, ImGui and event hooks; it does not implicitly own a Scene. `LayerStack` keeps layers below overlays. Events are offered top-down until handled. `Engine::GetScenes()` owns the active scene; `Application::GetMainScene()` is a non-owning debug accessor, independent of layer ordering. Scene requests are committed between event dispatch and simulation, never implicitly during script execution.

## Events and threading

- `Event` subclasses carry a category and type (window, key, mouse, gamepad).
- `EventDispatcher::ProcessEvent<T>` invokes a handler only when the event type matches.
- Any producer thread may enqueue an owned event. `EventEngine::DispatchPending()` runs only on the thread that constructed the queue, without holding the producer mutex during callbacks.
- Each dispatch drains a snapshot. Handler-produced events wait until the next frame, bounding recursive work. Stop rejects new events and discards queued work; producers must finish before the queue object is destroyed.
- Default event lifetime is unbounded; explicit zero TTL expires immediately. Pause holds queued events and resume restarts their TTL timers.
- Window callbacks clone payloads because their original stack objects expire before dispatch. Custom event types use `EVENT_CLASS_TYPE` (or implement `Clone()` themselves); event payloads must support copying or supply an appropriate clone implementation.
- `Application::OnEvent` handles close/resize, then forwards unhandled events to layers. Main-thread scene, layer and graphics access must not be performed by producer threads.

GLFW has no gamepad-button callback. After `glfwPollEvents`, `GLFWWindow::PollEvents` samples `GLFW_JOYSTICK_1` buttons and passes them to its fixed-array `GamepadButtonEvents` tracker. New presses emit `GpadPressedEvent(button, 0)`; held buttons emit `GpadPressedEvent(button, 1)` after 500 ms and every 50 ms thereafter, using a monotonic clock and at most one repeat per button per poll (no catch-up burst). Releases emit `GpadReleasedEvent`; a missing/disconnected gamepad supplies an all-released snapshot and clears held state. Reconnecting with a held button starts a fresh press/repeat delay. Events use the same window callback and queued cloning path as keyboard events, but retain gamepad event types/categories. Like raw keyboard callbacks, these raw events are independent of input-query enable gates and action bindings. Analog events are not generated. This event snapshot is separate from the existing `Input::Update` snapshot used by action/raw-state queries; taps entirely between polls cannot be detected.

`ThreadPool` runs queued tasks on a fixed set of workers and can return futures; `ThreadJoiner` joins workers before shared state is destroyed. Pool shutdown stops workers rather than draining all queued tasks. `ThreadRunner` is a separate reusable start/stop helper, not the application loop or event dispatcher. The legacy `DaedalusThreads` singleton remains available for compatibility but is not used by engine asset loading.

`Engine::GetJobs()` exposes its `JobSystem`, built on a dedicated `ThreadPool` with at least one worker. `Submit` accepts a callable, dependency handles and worker/main-thread affinity; only jobs whose dependency counter reaches zero enter an execution queue. Workers never block waiting for dependencies. `WhenAll` creates a group completion counter. Handles retain completion/failure state after scheduler destruction, and foreign-scheduler dependencies or waits are rejected. An empty/default handle is already successfully complete. Task exceptions are logged, mark the job failed and skip dependent callables; unrelated jobs continue. Empty callables, zero parallel-for grain size and submissions after `Stop` return completed failed handles.

Submission is thread-safe. `Wait`, `WaitIdle`, `ProcessMainThread`, `Stop` and destruction require the constructing owner thread. Owner waits pump main-thread jobs, allowing worker → main → worker dependency chains to finish even with one worker. Callbacks must not wait on themselves or their descendants, and must not destroy the scheduler or active caller-owned scenes/resources reentrantly. Workers express dependencies instead of calling scheduler waits. `ProcessMainThread` bounds direct executions by the queue size at entry; callbacks without explicit owner waits defer newly queued main-thread jobs to a later pump. Explicit waits may pump additional work. `Stop` is idempotent, rejects new work and drains all accepted jobs before pool teardown.

`ParallelFor` partitions indices into at most the worker count of non-overlapping chunks and returns a group handle; callbacks must support concurrent invocation and keep their captured data valid until completion. Chunk jobs and their group use bounded heap allocations, so this is not an allocation-free job arena. ECS transform preparation uses a serial path below 128 inputs and retained snapshot/output buffer capacity for larger batches. There is still no general asynchronous scene-loading API or automatic scheduler for arbitrary ECS systems.

## Platform abstraction

The rest of the engine uses `Window`, `Input` and `Platform.h`. OS-specific code lives in `Platform/Windows` and `Platform/Linux`; GLFW is shared in `Platform/GLFW`; the OpenGL implementation of the renderer API is in `Platform/OpenGL`. Windows headers must not appear outside `Platform/Windows`.

## Virtual filesystem and assets

Configured mounts are attempted independently; failures report the mount name, physical source and detailed VFS/libzip error rather than skipping later mounts. ZIP entry separators are canonicalized from Windows backslashes to forward slashes before safety and duplicate validation. Canonical collisions (including directory aliases) are rejected. Standalone archive reads validate the current archive directory and resolve the canonical reference to its entry index on that same handle, so mixed separator names and repacks do not use stale indices. Strict `ZIP_CHECKCONS`, traversal/symlink/encryption rejection and existing byte/count limits remain enabled.

`VisitSources` supplies a synchronous scan-scoped reader. `AssetRegistry::Scan` uses it to reuse one validated archive handle and canonical index for all source/sidecar reads in a mount, processing bytes one asset at a time rather than retaining the entire archive in memory. This removes repeated directory validation/opening for every registry entry. Readers are borrowed only during the visit and must not be retained or called concurrently. Each subsequent scan opens a fresh archive, including repacks with unchanged timestamp/size; there is no persistent timestamp-based index cache. Directory scans retain the existing physical read/sidecar-creation behavior. Standalone reads and unrelated model-import reads still open independent archive handles.

ImGui reads `assets:/fonts/calibrib.ttf` once through VFS (16 MiB limit) and creates its font from retained memory instead of a physical asset-root path. The layer owns those bytes until the ImGui context is destroyed; the atlas does not free them. Missing/empty font data is logged with its virtual reference and error before explicitly using ImGui's default font.

`Utils/VirtualFileSystem` serves UTF-8 virtual paths such as `assets:/models/example.obj` from directories or read-only ZIP archives. Engine mounts `assets`, `shaders`, `config` and `logs` from `PathConfig`; a configured regular `.zip` file selects archive reads, and `MountArchive` is also available explicitly. `Read` is the common byte API; `Resolve` returns physical paths only for directory entries. `Virtualize` maps contained physical sources back to virtual references, and `Join` normalizes relative model dependencies while rejecting mount escapes. Directory resolution rejects unknown mounts, absolute paths, `..`, backslashes, NULs and escaping symlinks. ZIP mounting/listing rejects unsafe or duplicate names, symlinks, encrypted entries and oversized archives. Limits are 256 MiB per asset/read, 100,000 entries and 1 GiB aggregate uncompressed archive data; metadata reads are limited to 4 KiB. libzip core is an explicit vcpkg dependency with zlib compression and no optional encryption/codecs. Reads open independent handles, check completed entry reads and never extract files. Enumeration is deterministic and excludes reserved `cache` directories and `.meta` files. Missing directory mounts enumerate as empty. This is not a race-proof security sandbox; physical-path APIs remain compatible.

`Core/AssetRegistry` indexes `assets` and `shaders`. Sources have adjacent `<source>.meta` sidecars containing `DaedalusAsset 1` and a nonzero decimal 64-bit UUID on separate lines (LF/CRLF accepted). IDs retain the ECS UUID representation but use a thread-local generator rather than its unsynchronized default generator. Directory sidecars are created through a temporary sibling and rename; ZIPs must bundle valid sidecars and are never modified. Invalid/unwritable metadata and duplicate UUIDs are reported, not replaced; all duplicate-ID sources are excluded. Moving source and sidecar together preserves identity. Records expose UUID, virtual path, physical path when available (empty for ZIP entries), source size, modification time and a 64-bit FNV-1a content fingerprint. ZIP record times refer to the container. Fingerprints are change detectors, not cryptographic integrity identifiers; collisions remain possible. Errors are accessible and logged. Existing valid sidecars permit read-only assets.

`Engine::GetAssets()` exposes the engine-owned `Core/AssetPipeline`. Pipeline APIs and registry views are owner-thread-only; record pointers cannot be retained across scans. `LoadAsync` accepts a UUID or virtual path and returns a handle covering worker I/O and ordered main-thread completion. Direct paths may read unregistered entries (result ID zero); UUID lookup requires valid registry metadata. `Bytes` returns binary-safe string data; `ShaderSource` recursively expands quoted includes relative to the shader mount, supports CRLF, spaces and trailing line comments, and rejects missing files, traversal, cycles and depths above 32. I/O/lookup failures use `AssetLoadResult`; scheduler rejection/task failure uses the handle and skips dependent callbacks. Callers keep callback captures alive until completion.

Startup initializes the registry synchronously. `Update()` schedules at most one worker scan per second; explicit `Refresh()` uses the same serialized path. Worker-owned copies read and fingerprint sources, detecting content edits even with unchanged timestamps/sizes, plus additions, deletions and UUID changes. Main-thread continuations publish records and deliver changes before simulation/rendering. Scans cover whole mounts rather than OS filesystem watchers; hashing adds source I/O, and ZIP repacks can conservatively trigger broader reloads through container timestamps. Accepted work drains before GPU teardown; standalone pipelines and resource managers also drain their injected scheduler before releasing callback state. The scheduler must outlive both. Callbacks must not destroy active services or wait on themselves/descendants. Scene activation/reload remains explicit; archive production is performed with external ZIP tooling, not an engine packing tool.

## Renderer

- `Renderer` (static facade, `Renderer/API/Renderer.h`) exposes `BeginFrame(camera)`, `Submit(model, transform)`, `Draw(...)`, `FlushPipeline()`.
- `RendererAPI` / `RenderCommand` abstract the graphics API; `OpenGLRendererAPI` is the current backend.
- `FlushPipeline()` executes `ShadowPass` → `DeferredGeometryPass` → `SSAOPass` → `DeferredLightPass`. A stack-local `FrameContext` carries submitted models, camera/frustum, viewport and texture outputs between passes. This is an explicitly ordered pipeline, not a render graph.
- After the deferred passes, G-buffer depth is copied to the default framebuffer. `ECS/Systems/RenderSystem` then draws scene skyboxes directly through `Renderer::Draw`; skyboxes are not part of the pass vector.
- Scene objects: `Camera`, `LightSource` types (directional, point, spot), `Geometry` (frustum, AABB, sphere helpers), `Cubemap`.
- Primitives wrap GPU objects (`Framebuffer`, vertex/index buffers, vertex arrays, `UniformBuffer`, `ShaderStorageBuffer`); resources include `Mesh`, `Model`, `Material`, `Texture`, `Shader` and `ShaderLibrary`.

`Renderer/Resources/ResourceManager` is an Engine-owned instance behind a static facade. Loading/upload and cache statistics are separate translation units sharing private state. All access and GPU-resource release must occur on the graphics thread; synchronous loading is not a worker-thread API. `PurgeUnused()` releases cache-only references, parents before their dependencies, at scene transitions rather than every frame. External `shared_ptr` references keep resources alive. Shaders remain in their library until shutdown/reload.

Shader-mount changes conservatively schedule worker source/include reads for root-level `.glsl` programs, including additions. `ShaderLibrary` applies only the latest generation on the graphics thread and preserves shared Shader objects and the last working program on failure. Successful OpenGL replacement transfers compatible uniforms, arrays and buffer bindings and updates cache/statistics. Directory binary caches carry a `.hash` fingerprint of expanded source, so startup checks contents as well as timestamps; ZIP shaders compile from archive source and do not write binary caches. Startup remains synchronous with existing fatal source/compiler failure behavior; reload compilation is nonthrowing. Both paths share `AssetSourceReader`. Removed/unregistered sources retain loaded programs. Graphics-independent tests do not validate GPU compilation/state transfer.

`Renderer/Resources/AssetImporter` produces CPU-only `ImportedModel` mesh/material snapshots and `DecodedImage` textures. A read-only Assimp I/O adapter resolves model files and material dependencies through VFS, including ZIP entries; workers decode external and compressed/raw embedded textures, transform node geometry and track opened source/material/texture dependencies. Models require valid triangle geometry, and decode/import failures leave prior snapshots untouched. `ResourceManager::LoadModelAsync` / `LoadTextureAsync` accept virtual paths or UUIDs; `LoadCubemapAsync` accepts six virtual face references and validates matching square RGB images. Handles include owner-thread upload and typed `ResourceLoadResult` callbacks. With no injected scheduler, standalone resource managers execute synchronously; async submissions to a stopped injected scheduler are rejected. Synchronous `LoadModelAsset`, `LoadTextureAsset` and `LoadCubemapAsset` wrappers wait while pumping owner jobs. Legacy physical loads inside configured mounts are virtualized into this path; outside mounts they retain the legacy importer.

Registry changes reload only affected loaded resources, using recorded model dependencies and cubemap faces. Generation/fingerprint checks reject superseded imports. Uploads stage textures, materials and meshes before model replacement; compatible texture/cubemap GPU storage is swapped into the existing shared object, and model contents/bounds move into the existing Model. Failed CPU imports or incompatible/failed texture staging retain working objects. Old cached meshes can remain until `PurgeUnused` at a scene transition. Clients caching raw GPU IDs must re-query after reload. Model reload does not recreate entities, scripts or model-derived physics colliders; use explicit scene reload when that reset is required. GPU buffer-allocation failures still follow existing renderer backend behavior and need real-context smoke validation.

Legacy model loading outside configured mounts retains owner-thread Assimp parsing and ordered worker-decode/main-thread texture-upload jobs. Imports inside VFS mounts use the CPU snapshot path described above. All stb sites use RAII/thread-local flip settings; failed decodes do not upload. Standalone managers without a scheduler operate synchronously. New typed async imports reject submissions after scheduler stop; synchronous asset wrappers can return cached resources but do not submit new imports during teardown. Raw/legacy resource operations keep their existing lifecycle behavior.

Exported facades hide subsystem state behind private pointers and use forward declarations. `Scene` retains a visible EnTT registry for the templated `Entity` API; public STL/shared-pointer types still require matching compiler/CRT settings. This is not a stable plugin ABI.

## ECS

`Scene` wraps an `entt::registry` and a UUID-to-entity map; `Entity` is a non-owning handle. Components are in `Components.h` and `SceneComponents.inl`. Newly created entities receive ID, tag and transform components. Scenes retain their name and primary-camera UUID; programmatically authored scenes can also resolve the legacy `Main Camera` name when no primary UUID is set.

`SceneManager` owns one active scene and one pending request on its owning application thread. A newer request replaces the pending request. At the frame boundary, it stops the old scene, transfers ownership and optionally starts the new scene; a null request unloads the scene. Failed runtime startup is logged and leaves the new scene active but stopped. Runtime startup requires a camera and an application/window. Pause suspends scripts and physics but still permits rendering.

`NativeScriptComponent` owns C++ script instances keyed by type. Scripts receive variable-step `OnUpdate`; the engine includes `NativeScripts/CameraController`, while clients supply their own scripts. `Systems/RenderSystem` collects lights, submits models and draws skyboxes. `Systems/PhysicsSystem` advances the scene's Bullet world during fixed updates.

For 128 or more renderable objects, RenderSystem snapshots transform components and retains model references on the owner thread into reusable buffers. `Systems/PrepareTransforms` computes independent matrices through parallel-for and waits before renderer submission. Workers access neither live EnTT storage nor GPU resources. A job failure is logged and recovered by computing the retained snapshots serially, rather than dropping renderables. Smaller batches, or a stopped scheduler, retain direct serial submission. Native scripts, registry mutation, lighting, skyboxes and Bullet simulation remain owner-thread work.

Each PhysicsSystem owns an independent PhysicsWorld. `Physics::CreateWorld()` uses the Engine-owned factory's default gravity; `scene.GetPhysicsWorld()` exposes scene-local operations. Body IDs are validated by their owning world and are never pointer casts. Components retain exclusive cleanup responsibility using weak world references, so moving/detaching a component or destroying the scene cannot leave a cleanup callback dereferencing a dead world. Runtime stop releases component bodies; restart recreates them from resolved creation descriptions. Bullet alone resolves contacts; collision notifications are delivered after manifold traversal and can remove bodies safely.

### Scene persistence

`ECS/Serialization` separates authored data from runtime entities, GPU resources, physics handles and script instances:

| Type | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `SceneRecord` | Versioned persistent scene/component records, stable entity UUIDs and asset-relative/virtual paths |
| `SceneJson` | Strict JSON parsing, validation, serialization and record file I/O, independent of graphics services |
| `ScriptRegistry` | Client-registered stable script names and property adapters for instantiation/capture |
| `SceneSerializer` | Instantiate/capture runtime scenes and combine those operations with file load/save |

Version 1 supports transforms, models, cameras, directional/point/spot lights, skyboxes, rigid/kinematic bodies and registered native scripts. The JSON implementation uses `nlohmann-json` privately in ECS; JSON library types are not exposed to clients. Instantiation/loading needs an empty, stopped scene and runs on the graphics thread after engine services exist; it does not start runtime. Capture requires a stopped scene. APIs return success/failure with an error diagnostic. See [Scene serialization](SceneSerialization.md) for the complete schema, validation rules and supported scope.

## Runtime assets and sandbox

`dlSandbox/ExampleLayer::OnAttach` registers client script adapters, loads through `SceneSerializer::LoadAsset(engine.GetAssets(), PathConfig::GetSceneAssetPath(), ...)`, and explicitly requests activation through `SceneManager`. Virtual scene references read directory or ZIP data; UUID loads look up bundled/persisted metadata first. Relative model/skybox references use `assets:/`, while explicit virtual references retain their mount. There is no compiled-in fallback or automatic scene restart on resource changes.

`PathConfig` resolves `AssetsFolder`, `ShadersFolder`, `LogsFolder` and `ConfigsFolder` relative to the directory containing `path.ini`, including defaults when loading a missing file. Runtime getters return resolved absolute paths. Saving writes these folders relative to the destination INI directory, using forward slashes and lexical paths without requiring assets to exist. Legacy absolute entries remain loadable and are converted on save; paths on incompatible filesystem roots (such as different Windows drives) remain absolute with a warning. Explicit `LoadDefault()` uses the current working directory.

`PathConfig` resolves `[Path] SceneFile` relative to `AssetsFolder`; `GraphicsConfigFile` and `KeybindConfigFile` are relative to `ConfigsFolder`. Saving preserves these bases, converting legacy absolute filenames when possible. The default startup file is `scenes/startup.scene.json` under the runtime asset root. Scene JSON, models, textures and cubemap faces are supplied manually. Files in `source/dlSandbox/scenes` are reference examples only, excluded from the sandbox target and automatic copying. Changing the configured startup scene does not require rebuilding the client. Installation packages the manually supplied runtime assets, not example scenes directly from source.

## Tests

`source/dlUnitTests/<Module>Tests/` mirrors engine modules (Config, Core, Debug, ECS, Events, Physics, Renderer, Threads, Utils). Every test file is listed in `source/dlUnitTests/CMakeLists.txt` and built into a single `dlUnitTests` executable registered with `ctest`. Tests must not need a GL context.
